Cajsar Otway, m his i a,er on " The Intellectuality of Domestic Animals," gives the following anecdote, which is bv far loo good not to receive the benefit of a wider circulation ;þÿ At the Hour mills of Tubberakeena, near (Jloomel, while iq the possession of aire late Mr. N. wbold, there was a goose which, by some accident, was left solitary, without mate or offspring, gander or goslings. Now it happened, as is common, that the miller's wife had set a numher of duck eggs under a hen, which in due time were incubated, and of course the ducklings, as soon as they came forth, ran with natural instinct to the water, and the hen was in a sad puckerþÿ her maternity urging her to follow the brood, and her sellisuiiess disposing her to keep on dry land, in the meanwhile up sailed tiie goose and with a noisy gabble, which certainly (bci. g interpreted) meant leave tin ni to my care, she swam up and down with the dm k lings; and when they were tired with their aquatic excursion she consigned them to the care ot the hen. The next morning down came again the ducklings to the pond, and there was the goose wailing for them, and there stood the lien in her great llustiuiiou. On litis occasion we are not at all sure that the goose invited the þÿ h e n observing her maternal troubleþÿ but it is a fact ihatste being near the shore, the hen jumped on her hack, and there sat, the ducklings swimming, and the goose and hen after them, tip and down the pond. And this was not a

solitary event ; day after day the lien was seen on board the goose, attending the ducklings up and down, in perfect comen'edncss and good humour, numbers of peot le coming to witness the circumstance, which continued until the ducklings, coming to days of discretion, required no longer the joint guardianship of the goose and lien.

To the Planters of Santa Croix, Gentlemen, It will he seen in my letter of the 29lh of October, that my remarks had reference to lite subject of the degree or amount of pulverization that should he given to the soil, as one of the conditions essential to its fertility, with my reasons for what was then advanced. 1 now recur to that pari of tire subject at which tiie limits uf my letter obliged me to break oil. It cannot he supposed that merely passing the Ploughshare through the soil, or dividing it by tire Hoe, can, miraculously imparl all that the soil requires for its productiveness. No. hut a certain amount of mechanical operations exerts t he most favorable influence, by lining lite soil for assimilation by plants, and it becomes i he more titled for this purpose, the more chemical action is produced ; which action is poetically called " the Tooth of Time for by it rocks have been, and are gradually reduced to dust (Hence the origin and formation of Soils.) and by it also soils are decomposed and with greater rapidity the more points of contact you present to litis external chemical action ; that is to say lite action of the carbonic acid and oxygen ol the atmosphere, severing and combining and thus cooking, (in homely plitase) the food of Plants. When we have recourse to tillage with a view to tlie.su lesulls we may he said to call iri the aid of science to guide our proceedings; in doing which, we merely imitate the conduct of the Physician and lite manufac-

turer ; whose successful career depends in n great measure upon the amount ol scientific knowledge that each respectively brings to hear upon the immediate object or objects engaging his attention. The application, however, of scientific principles to Planting, is, I understand, objected to, by many persons ; hut who, allow me to ask, should the mode of conducting matters on t lie part of agriculturists or Planting he less rational than that of those, whose time is given to other pursuits ? Science is a collect. on of the experiments, researches and investiga tions of, the conclusions arrived at hv the most studious and learned, the practical as wi II as theoretical who have lived in all ages up to the present lime And sue we to suit our eyes against light or informntjon dciived from such a source, and adopt in prefetenee the crude notions of those, who are wedded to their prejudices iri favor of practices that will ere long he as much contemned and ridiculed, as they are now valued and cher-

ished ? Agriculture in fact is h >!h a science and an art; and how the m ist important art amongst men can be successfully puisued without the enlightening aid of science, is difficult to conceive. What has brought t he manufacturing arts to the perfection at which they have arrived? The answer is science. Jn less than fifty years, Europeans surpassed tiie Chinese in those aits merely by the application of chemistry, but how inferior European Agriculture, even that of England is to that of China, which is the best in lite world! It then information or knowledge founded upon scientific experiment and research were applied to the cultivation of the land in lite spirited manner in which it lias been applied to manufactures, results equally beneficial and extraordinary would presently be ours, and the excellent system of cultivation in Chirm, the growth of centuries of experiments distinguishing the Chinese among the nations of the Earth, would soon he, equalled if not excelled by Europeans and others. In t tie hope that you may become shareisin the many advantages attending upon improvements in agiicullure. 1 remain, Gentlemen, very respectfully vours, 11 A. SMITH.

Gamer, veterinary surgeon, St. Ivors, was returning through Cambridge with Ins horse and gig, he had occasion to alter the harness, for which purpose lie stopped at the þÿ L i t t l e Rose,'1 but bad scarcely got out of the gig when the horse began to kick in a most terrific manner, to the imminent danger of a lady in the gig, as well as that of Air. Garner himself, who was holding him by the fiead, and a crowd of persons who had collected; but such was the fury of the animal that no one could render assistance. At last the brute threw himself fairly down, Air. Garner still holding him by the head, and affairs were in this desperate state when Air. Gox, chemist (next door), pouted about a drachm of chloroform on his handkerchief and applied it to the animal's mouth and nostrils. The gig and harness were then removed, and in about live minutes the effect of the chloroform passed oft, the horse got up, shook himself. and walked quietly into the stable. Aerolites.þÿ These are fiery meteors, which in various forms and sizes. are seen to shoot from lite heavens, and failing to the earth, are found to eonsist of certain kinds of stones. The chronicles of almost every age and conntry record t Ire fall of these bodies, which sometimes arrive on the surface of our planet individually, and at other tintes in what must be called a stream or shower, I lie celebrated Gassendi informs us, that, on the 2bth November 1 about ten o'clock a. m., while the sky was perfectly serene and transparent, he saw a flaming stone, tippa rentl v about four feet diameter, la 1 1 on Mount Vaision, in Provence, This stone was encircled with a zone of various colouts, like a rainbow, and accompanied in its fall with a noise resembling the discharge of artillery. It was of a dark metallic colour, extremely hard, and 59 lbs in weight. In June 10ti8, two stones, one of which weighed 000, and the other 200 lbs., fell near Verona. The event took place during the night, and when the weather was perfectly serene and mild, Thev appeared to lie all on fire, descending in a sloping direction, and with a tremendous noise. l ite phenomenon was witnessed by a great number of people, who, when the sounds had ceased, and their courage vias sufficiently re established, ventuicd to approach these celestial deposits, and found that thev had formed a ditch, such had been the force with which they had descended. One of the large.sl meteoric stones which have ever fallen, is now exhibited in a room

in the British Museum; it is several feet in diameter, of great weight, shaped like a spheioid, and brown in exterior appealanec. All meteoric stones that have been examined, ore-cut a similar structure and appearance Ttic chemical analysis of one which fell in France in 1M0. may he taken as a sample <>f the whole :þÿ Silica. 384 ; alumina, 8-0 ; lime, 4 2; magnesia, 130; iron. 258 ; nickel, 6 ; manganese. "0; sulphur, 5; chrome. 1-5: total, IKS 7. The velocity with which the stones are shot through the atmosphere tenders them red hot, and a- me time elapses alter their fall beloie they cool and can fie handled. With respect to the origin of aerolites, there are four theories, each having its suppollers According to Laplace, Potsson, Dr. llutton. ami others, they are stones projected from volcanoes in the moon ; it being demonstrated that an initial velocity of OlltfO feet per S' ootid would he sufficient to dijve litem bevond the moon's attraction, and to bring them wiihin the greater attraction of the earth Another set of philosophers allege thev are projected from volcanoes on the earth, which is exceedingly improbable. I'lavfair and others say it is not unlikely that the stones aitt formed in the atmosphere by an aggregation of particles of matter, the result of gaseous vapours; this chemical theory is also very unsatisfactory. The fourth and m -si probable theory is, that the stones are asteroids, or diminutive planets, drawn to the earth's surface when our globe,

in its animal revolution, arrives at points near which these bodies are performing a circuit round the s in. A scries of remarkable phenomena, of recent occurrence, serve to support this theory On the morning of the 12th, 13th, or 14th of November, every

J\ V It 0 25 J !3 . year since lstlfi these have occurred, at dill- rent parts of bo Is Europe and America, showers of meteoric bodies, ol a most brilliant appearance; and ti ftas t lichee been conjee lured thai the eaith, in iis revolution round the sun, haif fallen in with these bodies in the same or nearly th" same pan o| us orbit. If such be the true h\ poll.esis, it follows that these meteors are travellers in space, performing cirrous like the planets, and have most likelv been projected IVom the sun in the same itiaunet as the earth and other planetary bodies aie believed to have been hurled from that luminary. .Showers of fiery meteors, sometimes only gaseous, arid at other times solid, are, however, found to occur annually in August, December, and oilier periods of the year. In September 1811, a shower of many millions of meteoric stones, the greater number of which were not larger than small hailstones, occurred in Hungary, their elect incretheins being oxvdate ol iron, oxide of iron, and oxy hydrate ol iron, with flint, lime, and clay eaifh.

From Bei.e's Wbbui.y Mkssknobr, Loriooft, February, 14. 1848. Most Important þÿ Twri articles of intelligence of very great importance have just reached us. The first is a protest of the Emperor of Austria against t lie Constitution which has just been granted by the King of Naples þÿ His Imperial .Majesty will not recognise this (in his opinion) suicidal act against the legiti mate authority of all the monarchs in Europe; and as regards Italy, against the maintenance of peace and good order in his own states.þÿ It remains to he seen how the King of Naples will act ; but at all events the Emperor Francis can no longer pretend to any right to march an army to the aid of the King of Naples This will give the British Court full right to insist upon the observance of the integrity of the Neapolitan soil. The second article is a narrative of some of the stormy debates w hich have occurred in the French Chamfer of Deputies, upon a declaration of the Minister of the Interior, that the government had resolved to put down the Reform Banquets. M. Odillon Barrot, the head of the Opposition, and almost the standing chairman of all these Reform Banquets, denounced the present ministers as being worse than Polignac and I'eyronnet. All the Opposition deputies, to the number of 80, expressed their determination of going to the first reform dinner in the capital, in costume and in procession: and should they be refused admission into the bauqoettiog-room, to resign their functions as deputies en masse.
Unless the ministers give way, scenes of great violence are expected.
